title: CSP Heuristics, Forward Checking & AC-3
html:
Three questions make backtracking fast: which variable next, which value first, and what can we infer after each assignment. Good answers turn exponential searches into near-linear ones.

HeuristicRuleIntuition
MRV — minimum remaining valuesPick the variable with the fewest legal values leftFail first: tackle the most constrained variable before it becomes impossible
Degree heuristicTie-break by the variable involved in the most constraints with unassigned variablesReduces future branching (SA first in Australia)
LCV — least constraining valueTry the value that rules out the fewest choices for neighboursFail last: leave maximum flexibility — we only need one solution

Inference: forward checking and arc consistency

Forward checking

After assigning X = v, delete v-inconsistent values from the domains of X's unassigned neighbours. If a domain becomes empty, backtrack immediately.

Arc consistency

Arc X → Y is consistent if every value of X has some supporting value in Y. AC-3 enforces this for all arcs, propagating deletions until nothing changes.

MAC

Maintaining arc consistency: run AC-3 after every assignment during backtracking — stronger than forward checking.

AC-3

1
Queue every arc
For each binary constraint between X and Y add both arcs (X, Y) and (Y, X).
2
Revise
Pop an arc (X, Y); delete each value of X that has no compatible value in Y's domain.
3
Propagate
If X's domain shrank, re-queue every arc (Z, X) for neighbours Z ≠ Y.
4
Stop
When the queue is empty (arc-consistent) — or a domain becomes empty (no solution).

AC-3 runs in O(c·d³) for c arcs and domain size d. Arc consistency alone doesn't always find a solution (map colouring with 2 colours on a triangle stays arc-consistent), but combined with search it removes most dead ends early.

Local search for CSPs: min-conflicts

Start from a complete (inconsistent) assignment; repeatedly pick a conflicted variable and give it the value with the fewest conflicts. Remarkably effective on large, loosely constrained problems — started from a greedy initial assignment it solves the million-queens problem in about 50 steps on average, and it is used for real-time rescheduling.

Exploiting problem structure

StructureTechniqueCost
Independent sub-problems (Tasmania)Solve connected components separatelyO(dᶜ · n/c) instead of O(dⁿ)
Tree-structured constraint graphOrder topologically, make arcs consistent backwards, assign forwardsO(n·d²) — linear in n
Nearly a treeCutset conditioning: assign a small cycle cutset, solve the remaining treeO(dᶜ · (n − c)·d²)
Symmetric valuesSymmetry-breaking constraints (e.g. NT < SA < WA)Removes equivalent solutions
Explain MRV and LCV — why is one 'fail first' and the other 'fail last'?

MRV picks the variable with the fewest legal values: every variable must be assigned eventually, so discovering a dead end early saves work. LCV orders the chosen variable's values so the one that leaves neighbours the most options comes first: we only need one solution, so try the value most likely to succeed.

Forward checking vs arc consistency?

Forward checking only prunes the domains of variables directly connected to the one just assigned. Arc consistency (AC-3) propagates further: every arc is revised until stable, catching conflicts between two unassigned variables — like NT and SA both reduced to {blue}.

What is the time complexity of AC-3?

O(c·d³): each of the c arcs can be re-queued at most d times (once per deleted value), and revising an arc costs O(d²).
